rv.q: There are terrific speeches here and sizzling confrontations, and while it can’t be too long before someone snaps up this meaty material as a film property, it’s hard to imagine it ever again shaped quite so masterfully as in this dynamite production.
It is, flat-out, no asterisks and without qualifications, the most exciting new American play Broadway has seen in years.
Ferociously entertaining August: Osage County, the American dysfunctional family drama comes roaring into the 21st century with eyes blazing, nostrils flaring and fangs bared.
All the hallmarks of Violet’s character the implacable cruelty, the shrill self-pity, the wily manipulation and the will of iron are present and accounted for in Ms. Parsons’s superb performance.
Letts, a potentially great writer, is at his most brilliant and intense when he writes small chamber pieces.
This original and corrosive black comedy deserves a seat at the dinner table with the great American family plays.
Originally presented at Chicago's Steppenwolf Theatre, his account of a family whose secrets and lies come spilling forth under duress ranks with the best American drama of the past decade.
Tracy Letts' superb new play, August: Osage County, is not exactly a light evening in the theater. It is, however, richly rewarding.

With a transportingly elaborate three-tiered house set by Todd Rosenthal, and Shapiro's unforgiving staging, this production is a model of contemporary theatre at its most-daring and risk-taking best; whatever its financial fortunes, it's an unquestionable artistic success.
August: Osage County is electrifying theater, magnificently served up by the Steppenwolf Theatre Company and one of the most exhilarating new plays to find its way to Broadway in several years.
